1.sense: The surah opens on an oath, and the thing sworn by is a place. Not the sky or the mountains but one walled town in a dry valley, the town the speaker is standing in and the town that is in the middle of turning him out.

notes.t: The la at the front is read three ways: as a particle of emphasis that adds force and negates nothing, as a real negation meaning I have no need to swear because the matter is clear, or as a rejection of something the deniers had just said. All three are held by serious grammarians and the oath stands under each.
notes.src: at-Tabari and az-Zamakhshari record the positions without one being settled

notes.t: The city is Mecca, and the demonstrative hadha, this one, points at ground the first hearers were standing on rather than at a name they had to look up.
The Qur'an swears by this same town elsewhere and calls it secure there, which is the description this surah declines to repeat.

links.why: the same town sworn by, and called secure
Ibrahim asking that this place be made secure in the first place

2.sense: The oath is extended, and what is added is the man swearing. Something about him is unbound in this city. Read one way, its people are treating his life as fair game inside a sanctuary where even a hunted animal is safe. Read the other, he will one day walk back in with the restriction lifted for him alone.

notes.t: Hill is the opposite of haram. In a place where blood, game and cut branches are all forbidden, the word says that some restriction is off, and the exegetes split over whether it is off against him or off for him.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both readings, the second tied to the day Mecca was taken

notes.t: On the day Mecca was taken the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah made this town sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth, that it stays sacred until the Day of Resurrection, and that fighting in it was never permitted to anyone before him and was permitted to him for one hour of one day only.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, in the chapters on the sanctity of Mecca

notes.t: The verse raises what the oath is worth. The city was already sworn by; adding that this man is in it says the town matters partly because of who is currently walking around in it.

links.why: the promise of entering the sacred precinct in safety
those who bar people from the sacred mosque

3.sense: A second oath, and it swears by the plainest fact there is about people: every one of them had a parent, and every parent produced a child. No name is attached, so nobody listening is left outside it.

notes.t: Because both terms are indefinite, the exegetes differ on who is meant. Some read Adam and his descendants, some read Ibrahim and Ismail given that the oath before it is by their city, and some read every parent and every child with no one singled out.
notes.src: at-Tabari lists the three and inclines to the general reading

notes.t: The Qur'an says ma walad, what he begot, and not man walad, whom he begot. The looser word widens the range instead of naming a person, and Arabic uses ma this way when the intent is to cover a whole kind.
Placing parenthood next to the city is not decoration. The town is where lineage was traded on, and the oath swears by the bare relation while ignoring whose line it is.

links.why: the Day when no father pays anything for his child
the father whose prayer built the standing of this city

4.sense: This is what the oaths were sworn for. Man was made inside hardship rather than made and then handed some. The strain is part of the construction, which means a life without it is not a life that went right but a life that has not started.

notes.t: Kabad is the labour of something being carried uphill. The lexicographers connect it with the chest and with effort under load, and the early exegetes gloss it as toil, standing upright against difficulty, and being born already struggling.
notes.src: at-Tabari collects several glosses from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others

notes.t: The preposition is fi, in, not ila, toward. He is not walking into hardship from somewhere easier. The hardship is the medium he was made in.
The Qur'an makes the same statement in another surah, that man is labouring toward his Lord laboriously and will meet Him.

links.why: the same claim, that the labour is the human condition itself
the hardship named, and what is said to be with it

5.sense: A man who has come through some of that hardship draws the wrong conclusion from having survived it. He decides that since nothing has broken him yet, nothing has any hold on him at all.

notes.t: Yaqdiru covers both being able to overpower and being able to measure out and restrict. The question is not only whether anyone can beat him. It is whether anyone can set a limit on him.
The verb ahsiba, to reckon or suppose, is the Qur'an's usual verb for a confident calculation that is wrong. It is a man doing arithmetic, not a man in doubt.
The same root is used of Yunus, who is described as having thought that We would not restrict him, and the Qur'an then shows what happened next.

links.why: the same verb of supposing no constraint, applied to a prophet in a fish
does man think he will be left with no purpose

6.sense: The boast is quoted in the man's own words rather than described. He says he got through heaps of money, and the verb he reaches for is the verb of ruining a thing.

notes.t: Ahlaktu means I destroyed, and it is the same root as halak, perishing. He means to say he spent lavishly, and the word he uses condemns the spending from inside the sentence without the Qur'an having to add anything.
Lubad names things heaped and matted together until they hold as one mass, the way felt is made. It describes wealth that has stopped moving.

The exegetes name a man behind the boast, usually Abu al-Ashadd ibn Kalada or al-Harith ibn Amir, but the reports disagree and none of them is needed. The verse describes a type, and it is stated in the present tense, he says, not he said.
notes.src: at-Tabari and later commentaries record more than one name for the speaker

links.why: the man who gathered wealth and kept counting it
competing in accumulation until the graves are visited

7.sense: The same question a second time, with the delusion swapped. First he thought no one could reach him, now he thinks no one watched him. Both are conclusions drawn from feeling unobserved.

notes.t: Read against the boast just before it, the verse leaves two possibilities open and does not close either. Either he never spent what he claims and expects nobody to check, or he did spend it and expects nobody to ask what it bought.

The two questions are built identically, ayahsabu an lan and ayahsabu an lam, so the second lands as a repeat blow rather than a new subject. Arabic uses that kind of matched pair to say the two errors are one error.
Another surah puts the correction to this in a direct question about the same assumption, asking whether he did not know that Allah sees.

links.why: the identical charge, put to a man who thought he was unwatched
your Lord is ever in observation

8.sense: The reply does not argue about who was watching. It takes inventory. Two eyes were handed to a man who believes he was never seen, and the fact is put to him as a question he has to answer himself.

notes.t: The answer to a man who thinks nobody saw him is a reminder about seeing. His own eyes were issued to him by someone, and he did not build them, which makes sight a piece of borrowed equipment rather than proof of independence.
The dual form aynayn is used rather than a plural or a generic word for sight, and the next verse keeps the counting going. The passage lists parts, not faculties.
The Qur'an elsewhere puts hearing, sight and understanding together as things given to people who came out of their mothers knowing nothing, so that they might be grateful.

links.why: the same inventory of given senses, with the reason for giving them
He made for you hearing, sight and hearts, and little thanks is given

9.sense: A tongue and two lips, listed straight after the eyes. The equipment for taking the world in is followed by the equipment for putting something back out, and the boast three verses earlier was made with exactly these.

notes.t: A tongue on its own makes noise. Lips close the airflow and cut sound into words, which is why the pair is listed and not the tongue alone. The verse names the mechanism of speech in the order it works.

The same tongue that said I destroyed piles of wealth is the one being counted here as a gift. The surah will use the tongue again at the end, where people tell each other to endure and to show mercy.
The Qur'an names the teaching of clear speech as one of the first mercies listed in another surah, right after the teaching of the Qur'an and the creation of man.

links.why: speech itself named as something taught rather than developed
no word leaves the mouth without a watcher recording it

10.sense: Two roads were pointed out, not one, and the word for them is the word for high open ground that can be seen from far off. Both routes were made visible. The verse does not say that either was taken.

notes.t: Najd is raised, exposed land, the opposite of a hidden gully. Calling the two ways najdayn says the choice was not concealed from him. Neither road had to be discovered.

The great majority of exegetes read the two heights as the way of good and the way of evil. A minority among the early generations read them as the mother's two breasts, the first thing an infant is guided to, and at-Tabari records that view before setting it aside.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both, from Ibn Abbas and others, and prefers good and evil

notes.t: Guidance in this verse is showing rather than carrying. He was told where the roads go and left standing at the fork, which is why the next verse can hold him responsible for not climbing.

links.why: the soul inspired with both its corruption and its restraint
We guided him to the way, either grateful or ungrateful

11.sense: Shown the climb, he did not go up it. The verse states this flatly and gives no reason, and the reason is not needed because the previous verse already removed the excuse of not knowing.

notes.t: Iqtahama is not gentle walking. The verb is used of throwing yourself into something hard without stopping to weigh it, the way a rider drives an animal at a slope. The Qur'an does not ask him to consider the climb, it notes he never rushed it.

In Arabic la with a completed past verb ordinarily comes in a pair, and here it appears once, which the grammarians handled in different ways. Some supply an implied second clause, some read fala as a rebuke close to why did he not, and some take it as a plain report of a thing not done.
notes.src: at-Tabari and the grammarians record more than one account of the single la

notes.t: An aqabah is a road up a rise so steep that a loaded animal has to be unloaded. The image already contains the answer that verses thirteen to sixteen will give, which is that you get up it by putting down what you were carrying.

links.why: the parallel account of who is eased toward ease and who toward hardship
the loan asked for, and the multiplying of it

12.sense: The Qur'an stops and asks the listener whether he knows what the climb is. The pause is a signal that the answer is about to be given and that he would not have supplied it himself.

notes.t: Wherever the Qur'an uses this formula, wa ma adraka, the answer follows immediately in the next lines. The related phrase wa ma yudrika, what would make you know, is used for things left unanswered, such as the hour. The difference between the two is consistent across the Book.
The question is addressed to a single listener, adraka, and not to the boaster of verse six. The audience is being taught while the boaster is being examined.
By asking before answering, the surah takes the definition of a hard climb away from the hearer's imagination. Whatever he assumed the difficult thing was, he is about to be told something else.

links.why: the same formula, followed at once by the Qur'an's own answer
the same question form used of the night of decree

13.sense: The first item on the steep road, and it is not a feeling. It is a neck taken out of a collar: a human being owned by another human being, and the price paid to end that ownership.

notes.t: Two authentic readings stand here. Hafs from Asim, the reading this Mushaf follows, has the nouns fakku raqabatin aw itamun, the freeing of a neck or a feeding. Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr and al-Kisai read verbs, fakka raqabatan aw atama, he freed a neck or he fed. The first states what the climb is, the second states what he failed to do.
notes.src: the ten canonical readings; Hafs reads the nouns, Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr the verbs

notes.t: Raqabah, a neck, is the Qur'an's standard word for a person in bondage, and the choice of body part is not arbitrary. The neck is where the yoke and the rope go.

Fakk is untying and prising apart, not purchase. A report from al-Bara ibn Azib distinguishes freeing a slave outright from fakk ar-raqabah, which it makes helping toward the price, so that a person who cannot afford the whole can still be on this road. The report is recorded in the Musnad and its grading is discussed.
notes.src: Musnad Ahmad, from al-Bara ibn Azib; the gradings differ

links.why: freeing necks written into the fixed categories of zakat
the definition of righteousness, which also spends wealth on freeing necks

14.sense: The second item, and the day is specified. Handing out food when there is plenty is one thing. Handing it out on a day when everyone is short means the giver is short too, and gives anyway.

notes.t: Masghabah is not appetite. The root sagh-b is used of hunger that has gone on long enough to weaken the body, and the phrase yawmin dhi masghabah makes the hunger a condition of the whole day rather than of one stomach.
The verse names the act as itam, causing to eat, rather than sadaqah. It measures the deed by whether someone ate, not by whether something was given.
The Qur'an describes the same act in another surah as giving food while still wanting it, to a poor person, an orphan and a captive.

links.why: feeding out of a supply the giver still needed
the man condemned for not urging the feeding of the poor

15.sense: The one fed is described twice, first as an orphan and then as near. Near in blood, so the claim is one the giver could have argued belonged to somebody else in the family, or near in place, so it is a claim he walks past.

notes.t: Maqrabah covers both nearness of kin and nearness of location, and the exegetes accept both. Either way the verse picks the case that is easiest to defer, because someone closer or someone richer could always be said to owe it first.
notes.src: at-Tabari records kinship and neighbourhood, and the commentaries carry both forward

notes.t: The Prophet ﷺ said that he and the one who takes charge of an orphan will be in the Garden like this, and he held up two fingers side by side.
notes.src: Bukhari, from Sahl ibn Sad, in the chapter on the sponsor of an orphan

notes.t: Yatim in Arabic is a child whose father has died before the child reaches maturity, which in a society built on paternal protection means a person with a claim on everyone and a guarantee from no one.

links.why: the direct instruction not to crush the orphan
denial of the religion shown by how the orphan is handled

16.sense: The other recipient, described by his contact with the ground. The word comes from turab, dust, and it names a poverty with nothing left between the body and the earth.

notes.t: Matrabah is the last stage of a scale. A miskin already has almost nothing. Adding dha matrabah says he has no bed, no cover and no floor, and that what is on him is the ground he sleeps on.
Miskin comes from sukun, stillness. The word describes a person whom need has brought to a stop, which is why the Qur'an keeps pairing him with someone who must come and move him.
The two recipients in verses fifteen and sixteen are joined by aw, or, not by wa. The climb is not a checklist of everything at once. One neck, one meal, one child is a start on the slope.

links.why: the one who does not urge the feeding of the poor
wealth given, while loved, to the near of kin, orphans and the poor

17.sense: After the freeing and the feeding, faith is named, and then two habits that cannot be practised alone: telling each other to hold out, and telling each other to be merciful. The list moves from what one pair of hands does to what a whole group says to itself.

notes.t: Thumma normally orders time, and here it produced a long argument, because the deeds are listed before the belief. Most exegetes read it as ordering rank instead: after all that spending, the greater matter is that he was among the believers, since the spending counts only if he was.
notes.src: at-Tabari and the later commentaries record both the temporal and the rank reading

notes.t: Tawasaw is a mutual form. Each one counsels and each one is counselled, which rules out a version of this where the same person is always the advisor and never the advised.

Al-Asr pairs mutual counsel to patience with mutual counsel to truth. This surah pairs it with mercy, and it does so directly after four verses about slaves, hunger, orphans and the destitute, which is where mercy has something to do.

links.why: the same reciprocal counsel, paired with truth instead of mercy
cooperation named as an obligation of the group, not the individual

18.sense: Those are the people of the right, and the naming is short. The verse spends no words describing what they receive, only where they stand.

notes.t: Maymanah is built on y-m-n, the root behind the right hand and behind good fortune, so the word carries both the side and the blessing at once. English has to choose one, and the Arabic does not.
The Qur'an uses the same two titles as a pair elsewhere, ashab al-maymanah and ashab al-mashamah, when it sorts people into three groups.
The demonstrative ulaika, those, points back across five verses. The people of the right are identified entirely by the climb they made, and nothing else about them is given.

links.why: the same title used in the Qur'an's three-way sorting of people
the one handed his record in his right hand, and what he says

19.sense: The other side is defined by one thing, and it is not their hoarding or their cruelty. It is that they rejected the signs, which is what the whole surah has been putting in front of them.

notes.t: Mashamah comes from sh-m, the root of the left side and of ill omen, so it is the exact opposite of maymanah in both senses. The two names are a matched pair and were chosen for that.

Ayat are signs, and this surah has been listing them: a city, a father and child, two eyes, a tongue, two lips, two visible roads. The rejection in this verse is a rejection of things the hearer carries on his own face.
The pronoun hum is inserted before the predicate, they are the companions of the left, which in Arabic restricts and confirms. It reads as that is precisely what they are.

links.why: the same title given to the second group
the one handed his record in his left hand, and what he wishes

20.sense: The last word about them is a door. Fire is above them and it is shut down on top of them, which takes away the one thing every prisoner keeps hold of, which is a direction out.

notes.t: The root of musadah is used of a door bolted shut and of a vault sealed. The point of the word is not the heat, which was already named, but the lid.

The canonical readings differ over one letter here. Hafs from Asim, the reading in this Mushaf, has the hamza, muusadah. Other readers soften it to a waw and read muusadah without the hamza. The meaning is the same under both, and the difference is one of transmitted pronunciation rather than of sense.
notes.src: the ten canonical readings; Hafs has the hamza, Abu Amr and Hamza read it with the waw

notes.t: The surah opened on a city with walls that keep people safe inside them, and ends on an enclosure that keeps people in. The same architecture is used twice with the meaning reversed.

links.why: the identical phrase, a fire closed over, ending a surah about hoarded wealth
the fire whose walls surround them

1.sense: The first command given to a man who could not read, and it does not say what to read. It says under whose name to read, and it identifies that Lord by the one act nobody can claim a share in.

notes.t: Aisha's account of how revelation began has the angel take hold of the Prophet ﷺ in the cave of Hira and press him until he could bear no more, three times, each time saying read, each time answered that he was not a reader, and then giving him these opening verses.
notes.src: Bukhari 3

notes.t: Iqra is left without an object, which is why the tradition reads it as a command to receive and repeat rather than to decipher a page. Nothing was in front of him to look at.

The great majority hold that the first five verses of this surah are the first revelation. A minority named al-Muddaththir or al-Fatiha instead, usually by reading those reports as being about the first revelation after the pause rather than the first of all.
notes.src: the reports are collected and weighed in the commentaries and in the works on the sciences of the Qur'an

links.why: the surah the minority position names as first, and the summons that came after the pause
another opening command tied to the name of the Lord

2.sense: The verb of the previous line is repeated and then narrowed. He created, and out of everything He created the one instance named is the person being addressed, traced back to something that hangs on to a wall.

notes.t: Alaq is a collective noun from the root -l-q, to cling or be suspended. The lexicons use it of a leech, of clotted blood, and of anything that attaches itself. All three senses describe a thing that holds on to something bigger than itself in order to exist.

The order is deliberate. The creation of everything is stated first, then the creation of one species, then the state that species started from. A man told to read is being told what he was before he had eyes.
The Qur'an lays out the sequence elsewhere, from dust, then a drop, then an alaqah, then a lump of flesh, and it does so in order to argue about resurrection rather than about biology.

links.why: the same stage named inside the full sequence
the stages again, ending in another creation entirely

3.sense: The command comes a second time, to a man who has just said he cannot do it. The reassurance attached to it is not that he is able but that the One asking is the most generous there is.

notes.t: The first command was grounded in creation and the second in generosity, and the next two verses define that generosity as teaching. In this surah the most generous thing said about the Lord is that He gives knowledge.
Al-akram is the superlative of karam, which in Arabic covers giving freely, being noble in origin, and being above pettiness. The definite article makes it a class of one.
The Qur'an addresses the same worry directly in another surah, telling the Prophet ﷺ that He will make him recite and he will not forget.

links.why: the promise that the reciting will be supplied and retained
the gathering of it and the reciting of it taken as a responsibility by the One who sent it

4.sense: The generosity is spelled out and it turns out to be instruction, and the instrument named is the pen. Writing is treated here as something handed down rather than something worked out.

notes.t: A revelation given to a man who did not write opens by naming the pen. The Qur'an is not against literacy in the mouth of an unlettered messenger, it credits literacy to the same source as the message.
A qalam is a cut reed. The word is the name of a tool, so the verse credits the Lord with teaching through a thing, which is how most human knowledge actually arrives.
Another surah opens with an oath by the pen and by what they inscribe, and it does so at the point where the Prophet ﷺ was being called mad.

links.why: an oath sworn by the pen and by what it writes
the messenger described as unlettered, in the books the literate held

5.sense: The whole of what a person knows is placed on one side of a line, and the side it is placed on is the side of things received. He knew nothing, then he knew, and the change came from outside him.

notes.t: The sentence is built so that the verb taught brackets the man on both sides, allama al-insana ma lam yalam. Even the not knowing is stated in the same breath as the teaching, so there is no interval in which he was self-taught.
These first five verses say nothing about law, punishment or the hereafter. They establish who created and who taught, and the rest of the surah then deals with a man who forgot both.
The Qur'an makes the same claim about the beginning of a human life, that He brought you out of your mothers' wombs knowing nothing and then gave you hearing, sight and hearts.

links.why: the first man taught the names, and the teaching being what set him apart
the state of knowing nothing named as the starting point

6.sense: The tone turns at one word. Everything up to here has been about a gift, and from here it is about what the same creature does with the gift once he has it.

notes.t: Kalla is a word of refusal, and it is spoken to something not written in the verse. It answers an attitude rather than a sentence, which is why the surah can pivot on it without quoting anyone first.
Tugha is the verb behind taghut and behind the description of a flood that broke its banks. It is not sin in general, it is overflow, a thing going past the edge it was given.
The Qur'an uses the same verb of Pharaoh when Musa is sent to him, saying go to Pharaoh, he has transgressed, which fixes the word to a specific kind of ruler rather than a private failing.

links.why: the same verb used of Pharaoh at the moment Musa is sent
the peoples who transgressed in the lands and multiplied corruption

7.sense: The cause is given in three words. He looks at himself and concludes he is beyond needing anything, and everything in the previous verse follows from that conclusion.

notes.t: Istaghna is a form that means to consider oneself free of need. The Qur'an does not say he became free of need, which is impossible, it says he treated himself as though he were. The error is in the seeing.
The verse says he sees himself, not that others see him. Nobody had to agree with him for the transgression to start.
The Qur'an addresses the same illusion directly, telling people they are the ones in need of Allah while He is the one free of need and praiseworthy.

links.why: the direct statement of who actually needs whom
the one who withholds and thinks himself self-sufficient

8.sense: One line settles the matter without argument. The man who thinks he needs nobody is going back to somebody, and the direction of travel is stated as a fact rather than a threat.

notes.t: The address switches. The transgressor is spoken about in the third person, and this verse is said to the Prophet ﷺ, your Lord. The one who was told to read is being reassured while the other is being described.

Ar-rujaa is a verbal noun with the definite article, so it is the returning as such, not one particular trip. The phrase puts the destination first, ila rabbika, which in Arabic restricts it: to your Lord and to nowhere else.
The Qur'an states the same thing in another surah with a different noun, that to your Lord is the finality.

links.why: the same statement of where everything terminates
the end point of the hour placed with the Lord alone

9.sense: A specific person is pointed at and not named. The Qur'an describes him only by what he does, which is to stand between somebody else and an act of worship.

notes.t: Araayta is used in Arabic to make a listener look at a case and judge it. It is closer to consider this man than to did you notice him, and it is repeated three times across the next five verses.
Yanha is in the present tense, so the forbidding is a standing habit rather than one incident. The man is defined by an activity he keeps up.

The exegetes identify the man as Abu Jahl, and the reports around these verses attach to him, but the Qur'an itself withholds the name, which leaves the description free to fit whoever else does the same thing.
notes.src: the identification is in the commentaries and in reports; the text names nobody

links.why: those who bar people from the sacred mosque and from the path of Allah
the ones obstructing at the sanctuary who were never its guardians

10.sense: The object of the forbidding arrives one verse late, and it is not a rebel or an army. It is a servant, at the moment he prays, doing the one thing a servant is for.

notes.t: The Prophet ﷺ is called abd here, a servant, and not a messenger. The title strips the confrontation down to its bones: a creature turning to his Lord, and another creature telling him to stop.

The report tied to these verses is that Abu Jahl swore he would put his foot on the Prophet ﷺ's ﷺ neck if he saw him praying at the Kaaba, and when he moved to do it he backed away saying that between them was a trench of fire and something terrible and wings.
notes.src: Muslim, from Abu Hurayra, in the Book of the Description of the Day of Resurrection

notes.t: Abdan is indefinite, a servant, so the verse is not restricted to one man being stopped on one morning. Anyone forbidding anyone from prayer walks into this sentence.

links.why: instructions about how loudly to pray, given in a setting of hostility
the servant of Allah standing to call on Him, and the crowd pressing around him

11.sense: The question turns to the man being forbidden. Suppose he is on guidance. The sentence is left hanging without its conclusion, and the listener has to finish it.

notes.t: The apodosis is not stated. Arabic allows the answer of a conditional to be dropped when it is obvious, and dropping it here forces the hearer to say the damning part himself.
Ala al-huda uses the preposition of resting on top of something. In the Qur'an guidance is a surface a person stands on and error is a thing he sinks into, and the prepositions keep that distinction.
The Qur'an elsewhere puts the same either-or to opponents without deciding it in the sentence, saying that one of the two parties is on guidance or in clear error.

links.why: the same undecided pairing put to opponents as a challenge
whether anyone can guide one who is set on blindness

12.sense: A second possibility is added to the first. Not only might the man being stopped be on guidance himself, he might also be telling others to be careful of their Lord, which makes the interference wider than one prayer.

notes.t: The pair is exact. Being on guidance is what a person is, enjoining taqwa is what he does to others, so the two clauses cover his private and his public standing, and the forbidder is attacking both.
Taqwa is built on wiqayah, shielding. It is the care a person takes to keep something between himself and harm, which is why the word resists being flattened into fear.
The Qur'an gives the same instruction to the Prophet ﷺ about his own household, to enjoin the prayer on them and be steadfast in it.

links.why: the same act of enjoining, aimed at the people closest to you
a group calling to good and enjoining what is right

13.sense: The camera turns back to the forbidder. Suppose the one doing the stopping is himself a denier who has walked off. Again the conclusion is withheld, and again it is not hard to supply.

notes.t: Two verbs, and they are in the right order. Denying is a decision made inside, turning away is what the body does afterwards, so the verse traces the belief into the motion.

The third araayta has changed subject without warning. Verses eleven and twelve were about the man praying and this one is about the man interfering, which puts the two of them side by side and lets the listener weigh them.
The Qur'an uses the identical pair of verbs of the man who neither confirmed nor prayed, but denied and turned away and then went off to his family swaggering.

links.why: the same two verbs, with the walk home added
the one who denied and turned away, and what is prepared for him

14.sense: The three suppositions end in one question, and it is about knowledge rather than about punishment. The man is not told what will happen to him. He is asked whether he understood that he was being watched the whole time.

notes.t: The verb is left without an object. Allah sees, full stop, rather than Allah sees him or Allah sees what he does. Leaving it open makes the seeing a permanent condition rather than an act aimed at one person.
This is the same charge Surah al-Balad brings against a different man, who supposed that nobody had seen him. In both places the correction is a question rather than a sentence.
The Qur'an states the case in general terms elsewhere, that no three converse privately without Him being the fourth of them, wherever they may be.

links.why: the identical assumption of being unobserved, in another surah
the general statement that no private meeting is private

words.g: We will surely seize and drag

15.sense: The second refusal, and this time a consequence follows it. If he will not stop, he will be taken by the hair at the front of his head, which is how a struggling animal is controlled and how a man is humiliated in public.

notes.t: Safaa means to grip something and pull it hard, and the lexicons also carry a sense of scorching that leaves a mark. The word is physical and it is the opposite of a summons.

Lanasfaan is written with a light nun of emphasis that appears in the Mushaf as a tanwin at the end of the verb. It is one of only a few places in the Qur'an where this form is used, and it makes the threat a sworn one.
The verse says if he does not stop, not when he is judged. The door is left open for the man to change while he is still alive, and the report about Abu Jahl records that he did not.

links.why: no creature moves except that He holds it by its forelock
the guilty recognised and taken by the forelocks and the feet

16.sense: The forelock is described with two qualities that belong to the man and not to his hair. Lying and wrongdoing are attached to the part of him that is about to be gripped.

notes.t: Hair does not lie. Arabic can carry a person's quality across to a part of him, and doing it here means the hand closes on the man at the exact point his lying was decided, which the Arabs took to be behind the forehead.
The two adjectives split the offence. Kadhibah is saying what is not so, khatiah is doing what should not be done, so the description covers his tongue and his conduct without repeating itself.
The verse repeats nasiyah as an indefinite noun straight after the definite one in the line before, which in Arabic reopens the word in order to describe it. It reads as a hand pausing on the grip.

links.why: the seizing by forelocks named in the same physical terms
Pharaoh and those before him, and the sin the same root names

17.sense: He is invited to send for his people. The verse does not say he has nobody. It says go ahead and call them, which is a harder answer than saying you are alone.

notes.t: A nadi is the gathering place where the men of a clan sat and decisions were made, and Mecca had a famous one, Dar an-Nadwah, next to the sanctuary. The verse points at real furniture in the listener's city.
The command form here is not permission. Arabic uses the imperative to challenge, the way go on then is used in English, and the following verse supplies the answer to the challenge.
The Qur'an uses the same word of the people of Lut, who are charged with committing what is objectionable in their gathering.

links.why: the same word for a council, used of a group that did wrong together
a group saying we are an assembly that will win, and the reply to it

18.sense: The answer to the challenge uses the same verb. He calls his council, and the reply calls something else, and the sentence puts the two summonses in exactly matched language.

notes.t: Zabaniyah occurs only here in the Qur'an. Its root carries pushing and shoving something away with force, so the name describes what they do rather than telling you what they look like.
Sanadu is written in the Mushaf without the final waw of the verb, matching the shortened spelling of falyadu in the verse before, so the two calls look alike on the page as well as in sound.
The Qur'an describes the angels set over the Fire in another place as harsh and severe, who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them and who do what they are ordered.

links.why: the description of who is over the Fire and how they take orders
the guardians of the Fire, and their number given as a test

19.sense: The last word goes to the man who was being stopped, not to the man doing the stopping. He is told to ignore him, to put his face on the ground, and to come closer, which is the exact act the whole quarrel was about.

notes.t: Reciting this verse is a place of prostration, and it is one of the positions in the Qur'an that all the schools agree on. Abu Hurayra reported that they prostrated with the Prophet ﷺ at Idha as-samau inshaqqat and at Iqra bismi rabbik.
notes.src: Muslim 578

notes.t: The Prophet ﷺ said that the closest a servant is to his Lord is while he is prostrating, and told them to make much supplication then. The order of the two commands here, prostrate and then draw near, matches that.
notes.src: Muslim 482

notes.t: Kalla appears three times in this surah, at verse six, verse fifteen and here, and each one throws out a different claim: that man is self-sufficient, that the threat is empty, and that the obstruction should be heeded. The surah is built on those three refusals.

links.why: the prayer he was forbidden, now commanded in the last line
the instruction not to obey a sinner or an ungrateful one among them

1.sense: The last surah of the Book opens by telling one person to say that he is running to somebody. The one he runs to is named first by the relation that made him, the Lord who raised him from nothing.

notes.t: Uqba ibn Amir reported that the Prophet ﷺ said verses had been sent down that night the like of which had never been seen, and they were Qul audhu bi rabbil-falaq and Qul audhu bi rabbin-nas.
notes.src: Muslim 814

notes.t: Aisha reported that every night when he went to bed the Prophet ﷺ would cup his hands, blow into them while reciting al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq and an-Nas, and then wipe them over as much of his body as he could reach, starting with his head and face, three times.
notes.src: Bukhari 5017

notes.t: Audhu is a verb of taking cover. The Arabs used it of a person putting a wall, a tribe or a mountain between himself and what was chasing him, so the word admits from the start that the speaker cannot handle this alone.

links.why: the companion surah, which seeks refuge from harms that come from outside
the instruction to seek refuge the moment a prompting from Satan arrives

2.sense: The second title. A Lord raises and provides, and a King commands and can be appealed to when something inside the kingdom goes wrong. The refuge is being asked of someone with jurisdiction.

notes.t: Mecca had chiefs and Arabia had kings, and every one of them could be outranked. Naming Allah as King of mankind puts every human authority the fugitive might otherwise run to inside the same kingdom.

The three titles rise: Lord, who made and sustains, King, who owns and rules, God, who alone is worshipped. The scholars of creed use exactly these three relations to lay out tawhid, and they occur here in sequence in three short verses.
The Qur'an tells the Prophet ﷺ elsewhere to exalt Allah, the True King, in a verse about not hurrying the revelation before it is finished.

links.why: the same title, the True King, in a setting about receiving revelation
the King among the names listed at the close of al-Hashr

3.sense: The third title, and the one the other two were leading to. He is not only the one who made them and rules them. He is the one they exist to worship, which is what the whisperer is trying to interrupt.

notes.t: Ilah is the word for anything taken as an object of worship, which is why the Qur'an can say that some people take their own desires as an ilah. Attaching it to an-nas here says that of all the things people have worshipped, only one actually is their God.

Three verses, three titles, and each ends on the same word. Arabic does not need to repeat an-nas three times, and repeating it holds the listener's attention on the fact that all three relations are to him personally.

The three descriptions come without a connecting wa between them. In Arabic that makes them one continuous naming of a single Being rather than a list of three, which is why the surah never has to say that they are the same.

links.why: your God is one God, no god but Him
He is God in the heaven and God in the earth

4.sense: After three names for the refuge, one name for the threat. It is a whisper, and it is something that ducks out of sight when you turn toward it.

notes.t: Waswas names both the whispering and the whisperer, so the Arabic does not distinguish the attacker from the attack. The lexicons trace the root to the faint sound of jewellery moving, a noise at the very edge of hearing.

Khannas is built on kh-n-s, to shrink back and withdraw. The early exegetes explain it as the one who retreats when Allah is remembered and comes back when He is forgotten, which makes the remedy the same as the description.
notes.src: reports from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others collected by at-Tabari

notes.t: Both words are intensive forms, so they describe a habit rather than an incident. This is not something that happened once, it is what the thing does for a living.

links.why: the first whisper recorded in the Qur'an, and what it promised
the same whisper to Adam, offering a tree and a kingdom

5.sense: The place of the attack is named, and it is not the ear. It is inside the chest, which is why the harm in this surah cannot be locked out the way the harms of the previous surah can.

notes.t: Al-Falaq asks for refuge from what comes at a person from outside, the dark, the knot, the envier. This surah asks for refuge from something already indoors, and that difference is why the two were sent together.

A whisper is not an order. Nothing in the surah says the whisperer can make anyone do anything, and the Qur'an has Satan say on the last day that he had no authority over them beyond calling, and that they answered him.
Sudur, chests, is the Qur'an's usual seat of intention and of what a person hides. The verse locates the whisper in the room where decisions are taken rather than in the corridor of the senses.

links.why: He knows what a person's own soul whispers to him
the whisperer's own admission that he had no power, only an invitation

6.sense: The last line of the Qur'an widens the threat instead of narrowing it. The whisperer may be unseen, and he may also be a person you know, standing in daylight and talking to you in an ordinary voice.

notes.t: The Qur'an names both kinds elsewhere, saying that for every prophet there were enemies, devils among men and jinn, who inspire one another with elaborate speech in deception.

The grammar has two readings. Most take min al-jinnati wan-nas as explaining who the whisperer is, so a human being can do this job. A minority take it as explaining the chests in verse five, so that jinn are whispered to as well as people. The first is the reading of the majority.
notes.src: at-Tabari and az-Zamakhshari record both constructions

notes.t: An-nas closes this verse, which makes it the fifth time the word appears in six lines and the last word of the Book. The Qur'an began by naming its Lord and ends by naming the creature it was sent to.

links.why: devils from among men and jinn named together as one category of enemy
the first line of the Book, read against its last
